title: Should sport be compulsory at university?

turns.speaker: Adam
turns.text: The proposal is two hours of timetabled sport a week, for everyone, first year onwards. Non-negotiable, like a lab.

turns.speaker: Rachel
turns.text: I can see why they want it. Half our first years barely leave the building.

turns.speaker: Ines
turns.text: Then fix the building. Compulsory sport at school is the reason a lot of people never go near it again, and I'd include myself in that.

turns.speaker: Adam
turns.text: That's a strong claim. Is that actually true or is it just how it felt?

turns.speaker: Ines
turns.text: It's reasonably well documented, yes. Forced participation without any choice of activity tends to reduce activity later on.

turns.speaker: Rachel
turns.text: Although that's usually studied on team sport in front of your classmates, which is a specific kind of misery. It isn't the same as booking a swim.

turns.speaker: Ines
turns.text: True. The mechanism is humiliation more than compulsion.

turns.speaker: Adam
turns.text: So make it compulsory to do something, and let them pick what. Walking group, climbing, whatever.

turns.speaker: Rachel
turns.text: Then it's really a compulsory two hours away from a desk, and I'd support that.

turns.speaker: Rachel
turns.text: The health argument was never about being good at netball.

turns.speaker: Ines
turns.text: I'd still want an opt-out that doesn't require a doctor's note. Some people have reasons they don't want to explain to an administrator.

turns.speaker: Rachel
turns.text: Which leaves it barely compulsory at all, mind you.

turns.speaker: Ines
turns.text: Good. That's usually where these things should end up.

points: The proposal is two compulsory timetabled hours of sport per week from first year.
Ines objects that compulsory school sport is a documented cause of people avoiding exercise later.
Rachel narrows the finding: the research largely concerns team sport performed in front of classmates, so the mechanism is humiliation rather than compulsion itself.
Adam proposes compulsory participation with free choice of activity, such as walking or climbing.
Rachel supports this, noting the health argument was about time away from a desk rather than sporting ability.
Ines wants an opt-out not requiring a doctor's note, which the others accept, leaving the policy only nominally compulsory.
